rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this context shiqwah means abstract bad luck, the sinners’ futile excuse for their own failings.
rows.anchor: abstract "bad luck" (which is the meaning of shiqwah in this context)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The allegorical dialogue exposes a common excuse and indirectly stresses free will and responsibility for human actions and behavior.
rows.anchor: stresses the element of free will - and, therefore, of responsibility - in man's actions and behaviour.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to verse 10 of this surah and its corresponding note 11.
rows.anchor: See verse 10 of this surah and the corresponding note 11.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here al-munkar has the same meaning as in 16:90, as explained in the corresponding note.
rows.anchor: the term al-munkar has apparently the same meaning as in 16:90

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning addresses people who accuse others of moral failings while forgetting that only God's grace lets inherently weak humans remain pure.
rows.anchor: imputing moral failings to others and forgetting that it is only due to God's grace that man, in his inborn weakness, can ever remain pure.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad supplies an implied "ordained" in the literal rendering of the clause about God's name being remembered in the houses.
rows.anchor: Lit., "and [ordained] that His name ...", etc.

words: فِى بُيُوتٍ أَذِنَ ٱللَّهُ أَن تُرْفَعَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence implies that the spiritual purpose of worship houses is fulfilled by only some of their habitual congregants.
rows.anchor: the spiritual purpose of those houses of worship is fulfilled only by some, and not all, of the people who are wont to congregate in them out of habit.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayʿ literally means bargaining, selling, or buying and selling, and stands for anything that might bring worldly gain.
rows.anchor: Lit., "bargaining" or "selling" or "buying and selling" (bay') - a metonym for anything that might bring worldly gain.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For his rendering of zakah, Asad refers readers to surah 2, note 34.
rows.anchor: For this rendering of the term zakah, see surah 2, note 34.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers the reader to his note 133 on 17:111.
rows.anchor: See note 133 on 17:111.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God assigns each individual thing or phenomenon its function, an idea also formulated in 87:2-3.
rows.anchor: the function assigned by Him to each individual thing or phenomenon: cf. the oldest formulation of this idea in 87:2-3.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad's opponents implied that gradual revelation showed he had composed the Qur'an to suit changing personal and political needs.
rows.anchor: the gradual, step-by-step revelation of the Qur'an points to its having been "composed" by Muhammad to suit his changing personal and political requirements.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rattalnahu tartilan conveys assembling and well arranging the parts of something and giving it inner consistency; Asad compares 4:82 and 39:23.
rows.anchor: The concise phrase rattalnahu tartilan comprises the parallel concepts of "putting the component parts [of a thing] together and arranging them well" as well as "endowing it with inner consistency".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Consistency across the Prophet's eventful twenty-three years indicates divine inspiration, strengthens thoughtful believers, and is the deepest reason for gradual revelation.
rows.anchor: it is bound to strengthen the faith of every thinking believer: and herein lies, according to the Qur'an itself, the deepest reason

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When used of Qur'an recitation, tartil means measured diction and thoughtful enunciation, as in 73:4.
rows.anchor: the term tartil refers to the measured diction and the thoughtful manner in which it ought to be enunciated.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial particle bal expresses astonishment.
rows.anchor: The particle bal at the beginning of the sentence expresses astonishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's people evade his criticism of idol worship by stressing its antiquity.
rows.anchor: evading a direct answer to Abraham's criticism of idol-worship, his people merely stress its antiquity

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari argues that ancient usage and chronological precedence do not prove a concept sound.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshari points out - that "ancient usage and precedence in time are no proof of [a concept's] soundness"

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi calls the verse a powerful Qur'anic indictment of taqlid: blind adoption of religious ideas on a scholar's or leader's authority.
rows.anchor: Razi, for his part, states that the above verse represents "one of the strongest [Qur'anic] indications

words: وَٱجْعَل لِّى لِسَانَ صِدْقٍۢ فِى ٱلْءَاخِرِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally asks for a truthful renown or legacy among later people; Asad points to alternative readings in note 36 on 19:50.
rows.anchor: Lit., "grant me a language of truth among the others" or "the later ones". For alternative interpretations of this phrase, see note 36 on 19:50.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zamakhshari and Baydawi (with an attribution by Zamakhshari to Abu Hanifah) take this to mean that the Qur'an's essential teachings match those of earlier prophets; Asad says this accords with the Qur'an's repeated doctrine.
rows.anchor: is in full consonance with the oft-repeated Qur'anic doctrine that the basic teachings revealed to Muhammad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A more popular alternative says that the Qur'an was mentioned or foretold in earlier scriptures, with references to 2:42 and 61:6.
rows.anchor: Another, more popular interpretation is, "... this [Qur'an] has been mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people for whom this is evidence are those who disbelieve in Muhammad's prophethood.
rows.anchor: I.e., for those who disbelieve in the prophethood of Muhammad.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The learned Israelites include Jewish converts such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salim and Ka'b ibn Malik in Medina in the Prophet's lifetime, Ka'b al-Ahbar and Yemenite peers under 'Umar, and later converts.
rows.anchor: for instance, 'Abd Allah ibn Salim, Ka'b ibn Malik and other learned Jews of Medina in the lifetime of the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only learned Jews are named because the Torah survives in corrupted form, whereas Jesus's original revelation has been lost and cannot attest to the shared fundamentals of his teaching and the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: contrary to the Torah, which still exists, albeit in a corrupted form - the original revelation granted to Jesus has been lost

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to the account in 20:9 onward, especially note 7 on 20:10.
rows.anchor: Cf. 20:9 ff., and particularly note 7 on verse 10 of that surah.

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads the parable as showing that even a lowly creature may know something Solomon, despite his wisdom, does not.
rows.anchor: ignorant (Razi)

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari sees a warning against self-conceit, a danger especially acute for learned people.
rows.anchor: to which learned men, more than anyone else, are exposed (Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For background on the kingdom of Sheba, Asad refers to note 23 on 34:15.
rows.anchor: As regards the kingdom of Sheba, see note 23 on 34:15.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan here means people's immoral impulses, which persuaded them to evade accountability to a transcendent God and worship perceptible natural phenomena.
rows.anchor: their own immoral impulses (which is the meaning of ash-shaytan in this context) had persuaded them that they should not submit to the idea of man's responsibility

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hidden and manifest phenomena allude to the appearing and disappearing sun and other celestial bodies worshipped by Sabaeans and other ancient Semites.
rows.anchor: An allusion to the appearance and disappearance of the sun and other celestial bodies which the Sabaeans - in common with almost all the Semites of antiquity - used to worship.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse combines God's blessing of deep spiritual consciousness (ilm) with rational judgment (hukm), the ability to distinguish right from wrong.
rows.anchor: stresses the supreme divine blessing of spiritual consciousness ('ilm in its deepest significance) combined with rational thought, as expressed in the concept of hukm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad notes that nearly the same statement about Joseph appears at 12:22.
rows.anchor: This statement, almost entirely identical with 12:22

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses reached this spiritual maturity after the events of verses 15 onward, as indicated by 26:20.
rows.anchor: Moses reached this spiritual maturity after the events described in verses 15 ff.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madyan, biblical Midian, was inhabited by Amorite Arabs closely related to Hebrews, so its people could help Moses.
rows.anchor: The inhabitants of Madyan (called Midian in the Bible) were Arabs of the Amorite group. Since they were racially and linguistically closely related to the Hebrews, they could be counted upon to help Moses in his plight.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers to note 67 on 7:67 for Madyan's geographical location.
rows.anchor: For the geographical location of the region of Madyan, see surah 7, note 67.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term in the phrase about reaching the wells of Madyan literally means "water" or "waters".
rows.anchor: Lit., "water" or "waters".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal wording is "one of the righteous".
rows.anchor: Lit., "one of the righteous".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly enjoyments in question were misused gifts, wrongly credited to powers other than God.
rows.anchor: for having misused Our gifts and attributed them to powers other than Us

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase refers to people whom God enables to understand this divine writ.
rows.anchor: they to whom We grant the ability to understand this divine writ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jahada here means to deny or reject something one knows to be true, following Zamakhshari's Asas; Asad compares 31:32, 40:63, and 41:28.
rows.anchor: in the sense of a person's denying or rejecting something which he knows to be true is based on the authority of Zamakhshari's Asas

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yamin, literally "right hand," is a metonym for one's own hand.
rows.anchor: Lit., "with thy right hand" - the term yamin being used here metonymically, denoting no more than one's "own hand".

words: وَمَا كُنتَ تَتْلُوا۟ مِن قَبْلِهِۦ مِن كِتَٰبٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Muhammad could neither read nor write, Asad argues he could not have drawn his extensive knowledge of earlier scriptures from them; this should convince an unbiased person that it came by revelation.
rows.anchor: which - as the Qur'an points out - ought to convince any unprejudiced person that this knowledge must have come to him through divine revelation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubtil derives from abtala and can mean making a false or vain claim, trying to disprove or nullify something, or deeming it unfounded; the cited lexicons treat this broadly regardless of the target's truth or authenticity.
rows.anchor: unfounded", "false", "spurious", etc.; irrespective of whether the object is true or false, authentic or spurious, valid or unfounded (Lisan al-'Arab and Taj al-'Arus).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The li before yakfuru and yatarnatta'u signals a causal sequence, not purpose; Asad renders it "and thus".
rows.anchor: is not an indication of intent ("so that" or "in order that") but merely of a causal sequence; in the above context, it may be appropriately rendered as "and thus".
